passage:
Maths teacher's note, peer-tutoring hour, Class 10.
I paired Sonali, our strongest in algebra, with Tenzin, who had missed two weeks with a fractured wrist. Within five minutes Sonali had covered half a page. "Split the middle term, find the factors of ac, then just take common," she said, pen flying. Tenzin nodded, then stopped nodding. When Sonali asked, "Got it?", Tenzin said, "What's ac?" Sonali sighed loudly and turned to me: "I've explained it three times. Tenzin isn't even trying." I asked Sonali to explain it again as if to her little cousin, with one example and no short forms. She rolled her eyes, but slowed down. By the end Tenzin solved one sum alone. Sonali looked surprised, then a little sheepish. We'll pair them again on Thursday.

qa.q: Why had Tenzin missed two weeks?
qa.a: Tenzin had missed two weeks with a fractured wrist.

qa.q: Why did Sonali think Tenzin wasn't trying?
qa.a: Sonali felt impatient and frustrated; the steps were so obvious to her that she couldn't see that a term like 'ac' meant nothing to a beginner.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask Sonali to change, and why did it help?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to explain as if to her little cousin, with one example and no short forms, which met Tenzin at the starting point.

qa.q: What were the first five minutes like for Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably lost and embarrassed, nodding along to half a page of terms before having to ask what 'ac' meant.

grounding: Shows a teenager who knows algebra well rushing through jargon and blaming the listener for not keeping up.

passage:
Friday
Jahnavi asked me to help with the chemistry chapter on moles because the test is on Monday. Easy, I thought. I LOVE moles. So I told her: a mole is just a fixed huge number of particles, multiply by the molar mass, done. She looked at me as if I'd spoken another language. I said it again, faster, with the formula. She asked "what's molar mass" and I actually said "Seriously?" out loud. She packed up and left early.
Now I'm sitting here feeling bad. I was confused by this too, back in Class 9, but I can't remember HOW it felt. It all seems so obvious now.
Tomorrow I'll try it with a dozen eggs, the way Sir did for me. And I'll say sorry for the "seriously".
Yusuf

qa.q: When is the chemistry test?
qa.a: The test is on Monday.

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel after Jahnavi leaves, and why did the explanation go wrong?
qa.a: Yusuf feels bad and a little guilty; moles seem so obvious now that Yusuf can't remember how confusing they once were, so the explanation skipped the basics.

qa.q: What is Yusuf planning to try tomorrow, and why might it work?
qa.a: Explaining moles with a dozen eggs, the way Sir once did, because a familiar example builds the idea before the formula.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when Yusuf said 'Seriously?'
qa.a: Jahnavi probably felt small and embarrassed, which is why she packed up and left early.

grounding: Shows a teenager who loves a topic explaining it too fast with technical terms and reacting as if the listener were slow.

passage:
Faculty note, department seminar, 18 September.
Tushar, a final-year student, presented his water-quality project to the first-year batch today. His first slide read: "BOD, COD and TDS trends vs. WQI across three STPs." He began reading it at speed. Within a minute I saw phones come out in the back rows. Kishore, a first-year sitting near me, whispered to a neighbour, "What's an STP?" Tushar kept going, sure the slides were clear. At question time there were no questions. He looked irritated and said the batch "clearly didn't prepare". Afterwards I asked him how many of those terms he had known in his own first year. He was quiet, then said, "None." We agreed he'll rework the first three slides with plain words and one picture of a sewage plant, and present again next week.

qa.q: What did Kishore whisper to a neighbour?
qa.a: Kishore whispered, 'What's an STP?'

qa.q: Why did Tushar say the batch clearly didn't prepare?
qa.a: Tushar felt irritated and a little resentful, because the terms were so familiar to him that he assumed they were clear to everyone.

qa.q: What will Tushar change before presenting again, and why?
qa.a: He will rework the first three slides with plain words and a picture of a sewage plant, so first-years can follow from the start.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Kishore and the other first-years?
qa.a: They were lost within a minute, puzzled by short forms nobody explained, so phones came out and no one asked questions.

grounding: Shows a student presenter assuming first-years know his acronyms, losing them in the first minute, and blaming them.

passage:
Saturday night.
Today's talk at the community centre was a disaster and I'm still annoyed, mostly at myself. I'd been asked to explain our college survey on screen time to the mothers' group. I opened with "So our N was 240, and the correlation with self-reported sleep quality was moderate, not causal." Rajni aunty, in the front row, smiled politely. Nobody else moved. I kept going: p-values, sampling, Likert scales. By minute two a baby was crying and two women were chatting in Kannada. My face burned and I thought, they're not even trying. Then Rajni aunty asked, very gently, "Beta, so should my son keep his phone out of his room or not?" That was the whole point, and I hadn't said it once.
Next time: start with her question.
Nazia

qa.q: Where did Nazia give the talk?
qa.a: Nazia gave the talk at the community centre, to the mothers' group.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling during the talk, and why did it go wrong?
qa.a: Nazia felt embarrassed and annoyed, even thinking the audience wasn't trying, because terms like p-values felt normal to Nazia but meant nothing to the listeners.

qa.q: What does Nazia plan for next time, and why is it a good fix?
qa.a: To start with Rajni aunty's question, the practical point the listeners care about, before any statistics.

qa.q: How did Rajni aunty experience the talk?
qa.a: Rajni aunty sat politely through the jargon, then gently asked the simple question the whole talk should have answered.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using research terms the audience doesn't know, losing them within minutes and feeling resentful.

passage: The night before the society meeting in Chembur, Kavitha, a structural engineer, cornered her flatmate Siddharth on the sofa. "You know nothing about buildings, right?" "I play the tabla. She threw that out and started again: "Rainwater gets into the concrete, the steel rods inside rust, rust swells, and it pushes the concrete off, like a tree root lifting a pavement." Siddharth nodded. "Now tell it back to me," she said. He tried: "Water, rust, swelling, cracks." "And why fix it now?" He paused. She realised she hadn't said. She added one line about small repairs now being easier than big ones later. At the meeting the next evening, an old uncle repeated the tree-root line to his neighbour.

"Ma, I'm going to explain the login code thing, and then you explain it back to me. Deal?"
"Why me? Ask your office people."
"Because they already know. You're the real test." Nikita put the phone between them. "When you log in, the bank sends a number to your phone. Like a second key. Someone who steals your password still can't get in without the phone in your hand."

"Exactly! Now, when should you tell anyone that number?"

Nikita stopped. "No, Ma. Never. The bank never asks." She took a breath; that was the part she had skipped. "Say it back?"

I returned the story notebooks today. In Aparna's I had written nine comments: "lovely opening", "great describing words", "I laughed at the parrot" and more. At the end, one line in red: "Please check your spellings." At break, Dilnaz told me Aparna was crying in the corridor. When I found Aparna, she held out the notebook, pointing only at the red line. qa.a: It said, 'Please check your spellings.'

qa.q: Why did Aparna read the kind comments in a flat voice?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and ashamed about the spellings, and that one red line had grabbed all her attention, so the praise felt as if it belonged to someone else.

qa.q: What did the teacher and Aparna agree to do, and why might it help?
qa.a: Aparna will circle every green comment before looking at the red one, and the teacher will write corrections in the same colour as praise, so one remark doesn't stand out so painfully.

qa.a: Dilnaz was probably worried about Aparna crying and wanted an adult to help.

grounding: Shows a child fixing on one critical remark and ignoring nine warm comments from a teacher.

passage: In her dorm room in Toronto, Dalia had meant to check the weather. Two hours later she was still scrolling: wildfires, a drought, a species declared gone, a video of melting ice with sad music. Her essay sat open and untouched. When Amara knocked to walk with her to the dining hall, Dalia didn't move. "What's the point of an essay? It's all over anyway." Amara sat on the bed. "What did you learn in the last two hours that you didn't know at lunch?" Dalia opened her mouth, then closed it. Nothing new. Just the same stories, louder. Amara took the phone gently and set it on the desk. "Come eat. Then you can read one proper article, not a hundred clips." Dalia pulled on her boots, her chest still tight, but moving.

qa.q: What had Dalia meant to check before she started scrolling?
qa.a: Dalia had meant to check the weather.

qa.q: Why did Dalia feel that nothing was worth doing?
qa.a: Dalia felt anxious and hopeless because two hours of wildfires, droughts and sad videos made everything seem lost, even though she learned nothing new.

qa.q: What did Amara suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Come and eat, then read one proper article instead of a hundred clips, so Dalia stays informed without the endless feed raising her distress.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt finding Dalia like that?
qa.a: Amara was probably concerned and gentle, wanting to pull her friend out of the scroll without dismissing the worry.

grounding: Shows a young adult scrolling bad news for hours and concluding everything is hopeless while learning nothing new.

passage: The gram sabha meeting in Karad ran late, and old Jadhav had shouted at Vishal in front of everyone: the new milk collection time was "useless". Walking home along the canal, Vishal felt the words sitting heavy on his chest. At home he didn't sulk. He took down the green notebook where he and Charu, the cooperative's accountant, logged every week. This week: thirty-eight families delivering on time, no spoiled cans, two new members, and a note from old Mrs Shinde thanking him for the early pickup. One angry farmer, with one fair point about the timing for those with far fields. "So, one problem, not a disaster," Charu said, reading over his shoulder. Vishal nodded and wrote: 'Visit Jadhav tomorrow, ask about a second pickup.'

qa.q: What did old Jadhav call the new milk collection time?
qa.a: He called it 'useless'.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling on the walk home, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: Vishal felt hurt, the words heavy on his chest, but chose to open the notebook and weigh the week's wins beside the complaint instead of sulking.

qa.q: Which part of Vishal's response was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Planning to visit Jadhav about a second pickup, because it took the complaint seriously after putting it in its true place among the week's successes.

qa.q: How might old Jadhav feel when Vishal visits the next day?
qa.a: Jadhav might feel heard and a little surprised that his angry point about far fields was taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young organiser counting a week's wins alongside one loud complaint before deciding how things are and what to fix.

passage: On the last day of term in Manchester, Nadia carried the stack of student feedback slips to the staffroom. Last year she had flipped straight to the harsh ones and spent the summer chewing on them. This year she had a rule. She read every slip, then drew two columns on a sheet: 'working' and 'to fix'. Under 'working' went twenty-six slips: clear explanations, fair marking, the jokes. Under 'to fix' went four, three of them saying homework came back slowly. Jamal, marking beside her, glanced at the page. "That's a good year." "It is," Nadia said, and meant it. Then she circled the homework point, wrote 'return within a week' on next term's planner, and tucked the 'working' list into her bag to reread in August.

qa.q: How many slips went under 'to fix'?
qa.a: Four slips went under 'to fix'.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel about the year after making the two columns?
qa.a: Nadia felt genuinely satisfied and calm, because seeing twenty-six working slips beside four to fix showed that the harsh ones were only part of the picture.

qa.q: Why is Nadia's two-column rule a good habit?
qa.a: It gives praise the same attention as criticism, while still pulling out one clear change, returning homework within a week.

qa.q: How might students feel next term if homework comes back faster?
qa.a: They would likely feel that their feedback was heard and taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young teacher deliberately counting positive feedback alongside criticism before judging the year, and still acting on the criticism.

passage: Eshaan, you told Mummy your whole week was 'the worst' because of today's argument? Sit with your Hemant dada. When I was nine, my father asked me every Sunday how my week had gone. One Sunday I said, "Terrible. Master-ji is the meanest teacher in the world." Why? Because on Saturday he had made me stand for talking. My father didn't argue. He asked, "And Monday?" On Monday, Master-ji had let me ring the bell. Tuesday, he read us a ghost story. Wednesday, he gave me a star for my map. By Friday I was laughing. "So, one bad Saturday," my father said. I felt a bit foolish, and a bit lighter. After that, whenever anyone asked about my week, I started from Monday.

qa.q: What did Master-ji do on Tuesday?
qa.a: On Tuesday he read the class a ghost story.

qa.q: Why did young Hemant call Master-ji the meanest teacher in the world?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and angry about Saturday, and that fresh memory crowded out the good days, so it seemed like the truth about the whole week.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dada's story?
qa.a: His father asking about each day from Monday, which brought back the bell, the ghost story and the star and showed it was just one bad Saturday.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt if he had heard he was called the meanest teacher?
qa.a: Master-ji might have felt hurt or surprised, having given the boy the bell, a story and a star that same week.

grounding: Shows a child judging his teacher and whole week by the most recent day until the earlier days are recalled.

passage: The feedback forms landed on the desks with three minutes left before the bell. "Rate each teacher, one to five," the monitor called. Siddharth scribbled fast. passage: At dinner in their Kolkata flat, Payal asked Kiran how his week at Dida's house had been. "Boring," he said, poking his rice. "It rained and I just sat inside." Payal raised her eyebrows. "The whole week?" "Yesterday." "And the day before?" Kiran thought. The day before, Dida had taken him to the river to watch the boats. Before that, he had flown a kite with the neighbour's boys and eaten phuchka twice. On the very first day he had found a kitten under the stairs. His face slowly lit up. "Oh. It was actually good." Payal smiled. "So it wasn't boring?" "Only yesterday was," he said, and went back to his rice, already telling her about the kitten.

qa.q: Where did Kiran spend his week?
qa.a: Kiran spent his week at Dida's house.

qa.q: Why did Kiran first say the week was boring?
qa.a: Kiran felt bored and a bit glum about yesterday's rain, and that latest day crowded out the river, the kite and the kitten.

qa.q: How did Payal help Kiran remember the whole week?
qa.a: She asked about the day before, and the day before that, walking back through the week instead of accepting one word.

qa.q: How might Dida feel if she heard the week called boring?
qa.a: Dida might feel hurt or disappointed, having taken Kiran to the river and watched him find the kitten.

grounding: Shows a child judging a whole week by yesterday's rainy day until he is asked about the earlier days.

passage: Sharmila slammed the door of her room in their Hyderabad flat and threw her bag on the bed. Keerthana had told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were "messy". In front of everyone! "She's always been like this," Sharmila told her mother through the door. "Selfish. Showing off." That night, hunting for a charger in her drawer, she found a crumpled card: 'Get well soon, I'll bring your notes every day. K.' Class 7, when she'd been ill for a month. Under it lay a friendship band from Class 8 and a photo of the two of them at Keerthana's cousin's wedding, dancing badly. Sharmila sat on the floor holding them. 'Always like this' didn't fit. One mean comment today; years of notes, bands and bad dancing before it. She picked up her phone and typed, 'Can we talk tomorrow?'

qa.q: What did Keerthana say about Sharmila's slides?
qa.a: Keerthana told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were 'messy'.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel sure that Keerthana had 'always been like this'?
qa.a: Sharmila felt angry and humiliated, and the fresh quarrel felt like the whole truth about Keerthana, crowding out years of kindness.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that was wise, and what could she do tomorrow?
qa.a: She let the old card, band and photo remind her of the whole friendship before acting; tomorrow she could tell Keerthana how the comment hurt and listen too.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the quarrel?
qa.a: Keerthana may think the comment was just honest feedback on slides, without knowing how public and hurtful it felt.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a friend by the latest quarrel until reminders of years of kindness bring the whole picture back.

passage: Last winter I almost ended a six-year friendship over one afternoon. I'm Asif. Tejas and I had been best friends since Class 4. That afternoon, at the colony cricket final, Tejas ran me out, on purpose I thought, and laughed. I walked off the ground and blocked Tejas's number that night. For a week I told everyone Tejas had always been jealous of me. I really believed it. Then Ammi asked me who had stayed on the phone with me every night when Abbu was in hospital. Tejas. Who had lent me a bat when mine broke, and never asked for it back? Tejas. I sat there, stomach twisting. One run-out, and I had rewritten six years. I unblocked the number and called.
